title: Oswald Mosley
wiki_lead:
Sir Oswald Ernald Mosley, 6th Baronet (16 November 1896 – 3 December 1980), was a British far-right politician who rose to fame during the 1920s and 1930s when, disillusioned with mainstream politics, he turned to fascism. He was the Member of Parliament (MP) for Harrow from 1918 to 1924 and for Smethwick from 1926 to 1931. He founded the British Union of Fascists (BUF) in 1932 and led it until its forced disbandment in 1940.
After military service during the First World War, Mosley became the youngest sitting member of Parliament, representing Harrow from 1918, first as a member of the Conservative Party, then an independent, and finally joining the Labour Party. At the 1924 general election he stood in Birmingham Ladywood against the future Prime Minister Neville Chamberlain, coming within 100 votes of defeating him. Mosley returned to Parliament as the Labour MP for Smethwick at a by-election in 1926 and served as Chancellor of the Duchy of Lancaster in the Labour government of 1929–1931. In 1928 he succeeded his father as the sixth Mosley baronet, a title in his family for over a century. Some considered Mosley a rising star and a possible future prime minister. He resigned in 1930 over discord with the government's unemployment policies. He chose not to defend his Smethwick constituency at the 1931 general election, instead unsuccessfully standing in Stoke-on-Trent.
Mosley's New Party became the British Union of Fascists (BUF) in 1932. As its leader he publicly espoused antisemitism and sought alliances with Benito Mussolini and Adolf Hitler. Fascist violence under Mosley's leadership culminated in the Battle of Cable Street in 1936, during which anti-fascist demonstrators including trade unionists, liberals, socialists, communists, anarchists and British Jews prevented the BUF from marching through the East End of London. Mosley subsequently held a series of rallies around London, and the BUF increased its membership there.
In 1939 Mosley was implicated in a fascist conspiracy organised by the Right Club against the British government by Archibald Maule Ramsay.
In May 1940, after the outbreak of the Second World War, Mosley was imprisoned and the BUF was made illegal. He was released in 1943 and, politically disgraced by his association with fascism, moved abroad in 1951, spending most of the remainder of his life in France and Ireland. He stood for Parliament during the post-war era but received relatively little support. During this period he was an advocate of pan-European nationalism, developing the Europe a Nation ideology, and was an early proponent of conspiracy theories concerning Holocaust denial.

grok_lead: Sir Oswald Ernald Mosley, 6th Baronet (16 November 1896 â 3 December 1980) was a British politician and aristocrat who rose to prominence as a First World War cavalry officer and the youngest Member of Parliament in 1918, initially elected as a Conservative before switching to Labour in 1926. Disillusioned with mainstream parties' handling of economic depression, he founded the British Union of Fascists in 1932, explicitly embracing fascist ideologyâincluding antisemitism after 1936âand promoting corporatist reforms, protectionism, and opposition to war with Germany to preserve British resources and manpower, while its blackshirt paramilitaries engaged in violent street confrontations. The BUF attracted tens of thousands of members at its peak amid widespread unemployment but faced violent opposition and state suppression, culminating in Mosley's internment without trial under wartime regulations from 1940 to 1943. Post-war, he shifted to advocating a united Europe through the Union Movement, critiquing both NATO and Soviet blocs as threats to national sovereignty. Mosley's early career showcased innovative policy proposals, including deficit-financed public works and imperial trade blocs, which predated similar Keynesian ideas and aimed to reverse industrial decline through state-directed investment rather than free-market orthodoxy or socialist nationalization. His pre-war warnings against entanglement in continental conflicts emphasized empirical risks of attrition warfare, drawing from his frontline experience and analysis of Britain's limited manpower compared to potential enemies. His emphasis on economic self-sufficiency and avoidance of ideological crusades reflected a pragmatic realism rooted in Britain's island geography and imperial legacies, influencing later debates on globalization and sovereignty.
